2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not assessable / Not applicable: This is a single-country institutional and legal-historical policy synthesis reporting aggregate national and sub-sector administrative figures rather than tracking a cohort or panel of sampled units over time.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (weak control): Institutional and tariff reforms are described chronologically alongside major concurrent shocks—including the Economic Recovery Programme/Structural Adjustment Programme, high inflation, a US$240 million donor-financed Water Sector Rehabilitation Project, loan-to-grant conversions, and cross-debt clearing—without any analytical strategy to separate legal/pricing effects from macroeconomic and capital-investment confounders.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Strong-to-adequate: Primary Ghanaian statutes and legislative instruments governing water tariffs and sector governance are accurately identified by instrument number, year, and mandate (Act 310 of 1965 s. 2(2)(f), SMCD 85 of 1977, L.I. 1350 of 1987, L.I. 1597 of 1995, Act 522 of 1996, Act 538 of 1997), although de facto administrative compliance and enforcement are recounted narratively rather than measured systematically.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern (weak measurement transparency): Sector performance metrics (coverage rates, Unaccounted For Water, handpump maintenance recovery, and informal vendor water expenditure claims) are drawn from secondary government and donor reports without primary verification or consistent denominators; the authors themselves note that 1992 vs. 1998/1999 urban and rural coverage figures are non-comparable due to small-town transfers and settlement population threshold changes (5,000 vs. 15,000).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-adequate: Concrete administrative indicators (tariff schedules in cedis and US$, GWSC staffing, Unaccounted For Water, boreholes/hand-dug wells/latrines built, and urban/rural coverage percentages) are reported and key definitional breaks in coverage series are candidly flagged, but underlying survey/audit methods are omitted and key affordability assertions (e.g., low-income consumers paying >10 times official rates and >10% of income) lack cited empirical documentation.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No pre-specified protocol, search strategy, or source inclusion criteria exist, and institutional insiders synthesize grey agency documents selectively under 'Achievements/Successes'; however, this risk is partially tempered by candid reporting of persistent failures such as 50-57% Unaccounted For Water, government bill defaults, delayed tariff approvals, and non-comparable coverage declines.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (weak selection transparency): No formal sampling frame or source selection protocol is reported; illustrative regions, irrigation schemes (e.g., Tono/Vea, Weija, Upper East, Eastern Region, 41 rural communities), and unpublished donor/agency reports are selected narratively.

domain_ratings.justification: Accurately cites primary Ghanaian parliamentary statutes, military decrees, and subordinate legislative instruments with specific dates and provisions, including the Ghana Water and Sewerage Act (Act 310, 1965, s. 2(2)(f)), Irrigation Development Authority Decree (SMCD 85, 1977), L.I. 1350 (1987), Water Charges Regulation (L.I. 1597, 1995), Water Resources Commission Act (Act 522, 1996), and Public Utilities Regulatory Commission Act (Act 538, 1997).

domain_ratings.justification: Relies entirely on descriptive historical narrative and simple before-after administrative comparisons without a counterfactual comparator or formal causal identification strategy to link specific statutory or pricing reforms to observed sector outcomes.

While the text mentions major concurrent factors—ERP/SAP macroeconomic reforms, high inflation eroding delayed tariffs, US$240 million in donor-supported physical rehabilitation (WSRP), IDA credit moratorium extensions, loan-to-grant conversions, and cross-debt clearing—it does not analytically disentangle these fiscal and capital interventions from water pricing or legal-institutional restructuring.

domain_ratings.justification: Provides rich, granular analysis of Ghana's administrative architecture and political-economy constraints across urban, rural, agricultural, and water-resource sub-sectors, including ministerial tariff-approval bottlenecks, government agency bill defaults, decentralization to 110 District Assemblies, WATSAN committees, and farmer irrigation cooperatives.

Not assessable because the paper performs a narrative legal-historical and administrative synthesis rather than qualitative text coding or quantitative legal variable coding.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Gyau-Boakye and Ampomah (2003) present a single-country institutional and legal-historical case study ("information study") of water pricing policies and water sector governance reforms in Ghana from 1965 to 2002 across urban, rural, agricultural, and water-resources management sub-sectors. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (as a structured non-validated judgment with no numeric composite score), the study demonstrates strong legal source accuracy and jurisdictional/institutional specificity—accurately tracing statutory instruments (Acts 310, 522, and 538; SMCD 85; L.I. 1350 and L.I. 1597), tariff-approval mechanics, ministerial delays, public-sector arrears, and administrative reorganization (GWSC/GWCL, CWSD/CWSA, GIDA, PURC, and WRC). However, it has no formal Methods section, no primary sampling or document-selection protocol, weak measurement transparency (relying on grey agency/donor reports without audit details, though candidly noting settlement-base changes that invalidate 1992 vs. 1998/1999 coverage comparisons), no counterfactual causal identification, weak separation of pricing/legal reforms from US$240 million in concurrent donor rehabilitation and debt relief, and no reflexive discussion of the second author's insider role at the Water Resources Commission. Consequently, it provides valuable descriptive legal-institutional context but carries high risk of bias if interpreted as causal evidence on the impacts of water pricing or regulatory reform.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Strong descriptive legal-institutional documentation, but weak empirical rigor / high risk of bias for causal inference
raw_response.study_design_identified: Institutional and legal-historical case study (single-country descriptive policy, statutory, and administrative synthesis of Ghana's water pricing and water sector reforms, 1965-2002)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Appraisal grounded across the full article (PDF pp. 2-9): Abstract and Introduction (PDF p. 2); History of Water Pricing in Ghana and Experiences in Water Pricing (PDF pp. 2-5); The Reform Process and Achievements/Successes (PDF pp. 5-7); Future Perspectives and Conclusion (PDF pp. 7-9); About the Authors and References (PDF p. 9). No standalone Methods section is present.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper is not a randomized trial, quasi-experimental comparative evaluation with a comparator arm (single-country history cannot be forced into ROBINS-I), cross-sectional/cohort analytical study, primary qualitative interview/ethnographic study, mixed-methods primary study, or systematic review. Instead, it is a single-jurisdiction institutional and legal-historical case study combining primary Ghanaian water statutes and legislative instruments with secondary administrative performance data from government and donor reports, which directly matches the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.
